On the night of Ramchandra Ray's escape, Sitaram is an active obstacle: he guards the inner quarters, tells Udayaditya no one may leave, and only yields by letting Udayaditya disarm and bind him—protecting his own life and remaining loyal to the Maharaj. By the night of the prison fire, the roles are reversed: Sitaram becomes the facilitator, breaking Udayaditya out of the burning prison and leading him away, while Udayaditya, now a passive prisoner, is the one being rescued rather than forcing his way past. Once Udayaditya saved Sitaram's life (twice), prompting Sitaram's humble devotion; later that devotion is repaid as Sitaram defies the palace to free him.

Pratapaditya's initial plan was an ambush: he ordered that when Basanta Ray stopped at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore, two Pathan brothers would kill him on the road. The plan failed because one of the Pathans (Khan Saheb) refused to commit the murder—his brother instead led Basanta Ray's retainers away under the pretense of a dacoit attack, but Khan Saheb could not bring himself to kill the old man, warned Udayaditya of the plot, and threw himself on Basanta Ray's protection.

The method that finally succeeded was an official execution: Pratapaditya sent his commander Muktiyar Khan with a signed, handwritten death warrant for the King of Raigarh. Despite Udayaditya's capture and desperate pleas, Muktiyar carried out the order—Basanta Ray, accepting his fate, prostrated himself before his deity chanting on his prayer beads, said "Saheb, now!", and Muktiyar's soldier Abdul beheaded him with a sword.

1. In the inner quarters of the Jessore palace (the Mahishi's room), Ramai was disguised as a middle-aged woman; Rammohan exposed him, lifted him into the air vowing to kill him, tied him with a shawl, and carried him out like a sack.
2. In the king's room at the Chandradwip palace, as the king's jester, Ramai mocked the surrendered Vibha; Rammohan seized him by the scruff of the neck and threw him out of the room.

Mangala (Rukmini) prepares a slow poison disguised as medicine—obtained secretly by the Rajmahishi through Matangini to win back the Yubaraj's heart—and Surma takes it, dying by her own hand on the eve of her departure.

By the time she finally goes, Rammohan arrives bearing the news that the Maharaj is getting married that very day — she has arrived too late, and her hopes of happiness are shattered, leaving her a beggar-like outcast with no place in her husband's kingdom or palace.

Rukmini obtained the ring during her stormy-night visit: playing on Udayaditya's guilt and his desperation to keep her away from Surma's bed, she demanded "that ring on your finger," and Udayaditya pulled it off and threw it down for her. The ring bore a seal engraved with the Yubaraj's (Udayaditya's) name. Using this seal, Rukmini, Sitaram, and Bhagavat had a forged petition written — purporting to be from the Yubaraj to the Delhi Emperor, accusing Pratapaditya of treason so as to win the kingdom for himself — and stamped it with the Yubaraj's seal. Bhagavat then carried this petition to Pratapaditya, claiming he had intercepted it from a fleeing servant of Udayaditya who was taking it toward Delhi. Reading the falsely sealed document, Pratapaditya flew into a rage and, despite his minister's objections, ordered Udayaditya imprisoned — the genuine seal on the forged letter serving as the "proof" of his guilt.

The chain runs through Sitaram's dismissal and the stipend. Ramchandra's midnight escape was only possible because Udayaditya defied Pratapaditya's orders—overpowering Sitaram and the guard and opening the inner quarters by force. The aftermath of that night was the dismissal of Sitaram and Bhagavat from their posts. Feeling guilty that his defiance had ruined their households, Udayaditya quietly fixed monthly stipends for them. When Pratapaditya learned his son was aiding the very men he had punished, he forbade any further help; Surma then secretly continued sending the stipends through her trusted maid, from whom the matter leaked via Mangala. When word of this secret aid reached Pratapaditya, he retaliated against Udayaditya through Surma—ordering her sent to her paternal home—since forcing the women out was the only leverage available to him in the inner quarters.

The song expresses the desolation of an old man who has outlived everyone he loved—those who once answered his call are gone, leaving only emptiness. It is his lament for his lost family and the vanished joy of singing for them.

The two contrasting contexts:
1. In Raigarh, he hums it privately, reflectively, while watching the sunset alone—grieving that his loved ones in Jessore no longer come to him, even as his heart still leaps with the old joy that once sent him traveling to see them.
2. In Jessore, after finding the palace dark and empty—Udayaditya imprisoned and Surma's room silent and deserted—he sings it aloud while taking Vibha's hand, transforming private grief into a shared lament over the broken household before him.

Rukmini tried to warn the guards that Udayaditya was escaping with the King of Raigarh, but they ignored her, so the escape succeeded. Furious and humiliated, she reported everything to Pratapaditya — that Udayaditya had fled with Basanta Ray, and that Sitaram set the fire. Pratapaditya then dispatched the Pathan commander Muktiyar Khan with secret orders. In Raigarh, Rukmini tracked down Udayaditya and revealed his location to the soldiers, enabling his capture, and Muktiyar Khan then carried out Pratapaditya's written death sentence on Basanta Ray, who was beheaded during his evening prayers.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra with calm, unceremonious condescension: he shows no joy or haste, greets him with a flat "Come. Are you well?", ignores Ramchandra's attempt to speak by returning to ministerial business, and finally dismisses him with "Go now, my boy, to the inner quarters." The rebuff is delivered through effortless dignity and formality, and it works — Ramchandra "understood in what way Pratapaditya was superior to him."

Ramchandra's response, by contrast, is petty and dependent on others. In his own court he never directly confronts Pratapaditya; instead he lets his courtiers assault Pratapaditya's lineage daily — the Dewan recalling that Pratapaditya's father had to beg Ramchandra's grandfather for royal anointment, Ramai Bhand deriding Pratapaditya's ancestors as an "earthworm" and "leech," "kings for only two generations." Ramchandra simply smokes his hookah, smiles, and feels immense pleasure as these attacks are loosed each day. Where Pratapaditya asserted superiority through quiet, self-assured authority, Ramchandra can only feel superior through the borrowed malice of flatterers — a distinction the text itself underlines by calling him fickle, small-minded, and lacking the mental strength to either stop the mockery or stay out of it.

The widow is Rukmini, who later renamed herself Mangala and settled on the outskirts of Jessore. Bitter and envious, she befriended palace servants to track every piece of news, performed tantric rituals hoping for Pratapaditya's and Surma's deaths, and dreamed of ruling Udayaditya's heart and the kingdom when he ascended the throne. When the Rajmahishi sought a way to send Surma away, Mangala, posing as a widow skilled in tantra and medicine, prepared a slow poison—taking five days so that mantras would ensure Udayaditya felt no pity—delivered through Matangini. Surma took it and died in Udayaditya's arms. Later, exploiting his lingering guilt over their past, Rukmini entered his darkened bedchamber on a stormy night, wept that he had ruined her, and extorted a ring from him, deepening his grief and leaving the door open for further schemes (including plotting with Sitaram).

In Chapter 1, Udayaditya laments being born an heir rather than a son—tested like an examinee, judged a fool, despised as unfit to rule—and wishes he could undo his birth into royalty. By Chapter 34, that alienation culminates after his catastrophe: brought back as a prisoner, he declares himself unworthy of the kingdom, formally renounces the throne by swearing before Ma-Kali that he will never rule even a needle's tip of his father's land and will never touch the royal scepter, naming Samaraditya as heir. He asks only release from the throne and money to establish a guest house and temple in his grand-uncle's name in Kashi—transforming the boy who once wished he had never been born into a prince who willingly abandons the crown entirely.

Ramchandra Ray writes to Pratapaditya renouncing Vibha and forbidding her from being sent to Chandradwip again. Rammohan refuses to carry it, so old Nayanchand takes the letter—but fearing Pratapaditya's reaction, he secretly gives it to the Mahishi instead of delivering it. She hides it from the Maharaj (mentioning to him only a hypothetical "what if our son-in-law abandons Vibha," which he dismisses as speculation), since she fears the letter would kill the delicate Vibha. Later she shows it to Basanta Ray, who advises keeping its contents secret and announcing throughout the household that Ramchandra has written *requesting* that Vibha be sent to her in-laws. Thus deceived into believing her husband has forgiven her and summoned her, Vibha's sorrow turns to joy.

Pratapaditya blocks the canal adjoining the palace with large sal-wood logs, hoping to trap Ramchandra Ray's boat. The trap fails because the guards cannot stop the boat once it appears: their stones fall short, they have only swords (no guns), and the single flintlock they find is useless for lack of gunpowder and bullets. While they shout for ammunition, Rammohan and his followers simply drag the boat up and over the log barrier. The pursuit also collapses when the man sent to fetch a chase-boat detours to Harimudi's shop to smoke a pipe and to wake Ramashankar over a debt, so the boat arrives long after any chance of catching the fugitives is gone.

Basanta Ray's sitar traces the arc of his despair. In Chapter 13, at the moment of his forced separation from Udayaditya, he still clings to music in anguish—he seizes the sitar and plays it furiously to drown his grief, but even that fails him: his eyes blur with tears, his throat chokes, and he abandons it. Leaving Jessore, he deliberately leaves the sitar behind, saying "I will not play it anymore"—as if the instrument belonged to a life with Udayaditya that has now ended, and his parting song ("my time to leave has come... don't bind me in the threads of affection") becomes its farewell performance.

In Chapter 27, in exile at Raigarh, the sitar's meaning deepens: Khan Saheb notes it is absent, and Basanta Ray replies that the sitar is still there, but its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned. The broken instrument is a metaphor for himself—he survives, but the "strings" binding him to his loved ones (above all to Udayaditya, whom he sang for) are severed. He can still sing "I alone am left behind" with his voice, and briefly revive when he joins Khan Saheb's song, but the sitar—the emblem of the joy he once shared with Udayaditya—remains untunable. Thus the sitar's fate mirrors his own: from furious playing against grief, to abandonment at parting, to a broken, unstrung silence, ending with his cry "Dada, come to me! No one understood you."

Before Surma's death, Udayaditya was fearless and decisive: he treated danger as a trifle, fought oppression with all his might, and would stop an abusive official on the spot without considering the consequences. He also openly and secretly helped those in need,
Earlier, Udayaditya was fearless: he treated danger as a trifle, fought oppression with all his might, and would stop an abusive official on the spot without considering the consequences, openly or secretly helping those in need. After Surma's death, a blind fear of Pratapaditya took hold of him—his courage vanished, and doubt arose in every matter. Hearing of the planned raid on the Chhapra zamindar's office, he ordered his horse readied but then absently told the servant to take it away. Hearing a subject tied to a tree cry "Mercy, Yubaraj!" as an official beat him, he could not bear the sight and fled into his house instead of intervening. He even lost the nerve to keep sending money to Bhagavat and Sitaram, repeatedly intending to send it but always hesitating. The narrator stresses this was not fear for his own life, but regarding Pratapaditya as a mysterious entity whose will governed even his final moments, as if his whole fate lay in Pratapaditya's fist.

Sitaram had caused Udayaditya's imprisonment by helping Bhagavat forge the treason petition. He undoes this by staging a fire in the row of guard huts beside the prison: while the guards rush off to fight the blaze, their customary, lax watch over Udayaditya dissolves. Sitaram then enters the dark cell, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and carries him out to the open field—freeing him. He also quietly leads Basanta Ray out of the palace that same night (refusing to let him first visit Vibha, saying there is no time), bringing the two together so that Udayaditya's escape—made possible by the very fire Sitaram engineered—reverses the injustice born of the forged petition.

**Occasion 1 – Pratapaditya's palace in Jessore (Chapter 11):** To rescue Ramchandra Ray after Udayaditya smuggled him to the roof, Rammohan gathers several very thick, large bed sheets, twists and ties them together into a huge rope, and fastens it to a small pillar on the roof overlooking the canal (about seventy cubits below), where Ramchandra's sixty-four-oared boat floats. Despite everyone's protests that it is impossible, he bows to the family crying "Victory to Ma-Kali!", lifts Ramchandra onto his back, and climbs down the rope. At the rope's end he grips it with his teeth, frees his hands, carefully lowers the clinging, eyes-closed Ramchandra into the boat, and then jumps down himself—escaping over the log-blocked canal as the guards, delayed by the search for a flintlock and gunpowder, futilely hurl stones.

**Occasion 2 – Ramchandra Ray's palace in Chandradwip (Chapter 37):** When Vibha, insulted by the king and the jester, faints on the palace floor, Rammohan renounces his family's four-generation service, bows to the king, then lifts the unconscious Vibha in his arms, carries her out of the palace past the gate, and places her in one of the many palanquins standing near the gate—removing her physically before she can recover.

In Jessore, Vibha is adorned as a lavish bride-to-be: the Mahishi dresses her with her own hands, forcing on her eight thick gold bangles and a huge diamond bracelet on each arm, a large nose ring she knows doesn't suit her, and an elaborate hairstyle redone to the queen's taste—then displays her to the elderly maidservants and widowed aunts. She is the celebrated center of attention, her joy visible to all, welcomed as the bride of the Yubaraj in a palace busy with festive preparations.

In Chandradwip, the presentation is deliberately stripped of all royalty. She refuses a palanquin—"Am I a queen that I should ask for a palanquin?"—and dresses as a common woman, saying she will go "like a beggar-woman." Her veil slips at the palace gate and she must hastily cover herself in shame; the guard grabs her hand, no one welcomes her, and she enters "like any other maidservant." Unrecognized, she falls at Ramchandra's feet and is mistaken for a beggar seeking alms—the woman once loaded with gold and diamonds arrives with nothing, offering to surrender her husband "into another's hands."

In the bedchamber after Surma's death, the window is a symbol of absence and grief: it marks the spot she used to occupy, and Udayaditya leaves it empty, drawn to it by the futile hope that in the same moonlight, the same garden, and the same breeze she cannot possibly stay away. Looking through it, he even imagines he hears her voice; the window frames a beauty that only deepens his loss and his waiting for someone who will not return.

In the prison cell, the window's meaning inverts into a symbol of hope and inner freedom. It is now a tiny opening cut into a wall, showing only a sliver of sky, a bamboo grove, and a Shiva temple—yet Udayaditya chooses the floor beside it over the soft cot, because through it he watches birds fly and believes his own cage, too, will one day break and he will "swim in that endless sky." Away from the window, surrounded by darkness, he forgets he will ever be free; near it, he knows that "no king or emperor" can hold him captive. Thus the window shifts from a memorial of irreplaceable loss to a lifeline of liberation—paradoxically, the window in the real prison frees his spirit, while the window in his own chamber had only imprisoned him in grief.

In Chapter 21 the relationship is a transactional flirtation: the penniless, self-styled wit Sitaram borrows from the widow-moneylender Rukmini, flattering her with mock-romantic endearments ("Pran... Priye... Pranpriye"), dodging the subject of interest, and even becoming her secret co-conspirator in a scheme. Money and vanity bind them—she lends, he performs affection he doesn't feel.

The first rupture comes after Udayaditya's imprisonment: Sitaram storms into her house, curses her, nearly strikes her, and vows to burn her home, deface her with lime and soot, and drive her from the city before leaving for Raigarh. Rukmini restrains a trembling, demonic rage and reframes the quarrel as possessive rivalry—Udayaditya is "my Yubaraj," whom only she can save or destroy.

By their last encounter, it has turned lethal. After faking the Yubaraj's death in the prison fire, Sitaram goes to rob the widowed "Mangala" and finds her seemingly risen from the dead—soaked, ash-faced, spectral—declaring she has "returned from the door of Yama" and will burn him and the Yubaraj and consecrate herself with their ashes. His old currency of feigned affection ("Shall I sing that song?") now only feeds her fury; she goes to fetch a curved blade to kill him, and he flees while she hacks the floor where he stood. The flirtatious lender-borrower game ends in a knife attack, her vengeful betrayal of the whole plot to Pratapaditya, and Sitaram's flight from Jessore—affection and money having curdled into mutual ruin.

Sitaram's scheme escalates in three deliberate stages, each layer of fire serving a larger purpose:

1. **Distraction to enable the escape.** The initial blaze — five or six rooms igniting "simultaneously" in the evening, no accident — draws the palace's attention away from Udayaditya's door, which was only nominally guarded because the prince sat so quietly that the guards felt free to be the first to run. Sitaram deepens the diversion by planting his own men among the firefighters: they pour water where there is no fire, fetch water without returning it, smash their pots, and stumble into one another, ensuring the chaos lasts long enough for him to enter the prison, "rescue" Udayaditya under the pretext that the prison itself is burning, and lead him to the boat.

2. **Destroying the evidence of escape.** Once the Yubaraj is away, the strategy shifts from distraction to fabrication. Sitaram's men torch the empty cell — windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, wooden fences — a fire no one imagines could start there, so no one questions it. Into the burning room Sitaram throws bones, a skull, and Udayaditya's sword, physically staging a corpse and its belongings. Shouts are staged that the Yubaraj is screaming and that the roof has collapsed with no response from him, converting a suspicious absence into a believable death.

3. **Controlling the narrative and witnesses.** Before the fire even, he sends three of Udayaditya's letters to the palace with a man secretly ordered never to deliver them, then retrieves them and destroys all but those for the Mahishi and Vibha — eliminating incriminating paper while preserving sentimental proof. He calculates that the rumor of death in the fire will "remain untroubled for some time," and when it reaches Pratapaditya's court, the staged evidence works exactly as designed: witnesses testify to seeing the Yubaraj through the window and hearing screams, and the melted sword is produced. Only the loose thread of Rukmini/Mangala, who knows everything, forces the final evolution — he abandons concealment for flight, escaping Jessore that very night with his family to Raigarh.

In short, the fire grows from a smokescreen to free the prince, into a funeral pyre that fakes his death, and finally into a broken cover-up whose surviving witness forces Sitaram to trade deception for disappearance.

Ramchandra Ray dismisses Udayaditya's heroism entirely: he believes Udayaditya saved him only for the sake of his own sister (Vibha), not out of any genuine loyalty to him, and that the rescue was something bound to happen anyway—anyone in his place would have been saved by everyone. Feeling no debt of gratitude, he readily joins the court's mockery, ridiculing Udayaditya in court solely for the "crime" of being Pratapaditya's son.

In Chapter 2, Pratapaditya mocks the minister's repeated warnings about the Emperor of Delhi—"The Emperor of Delhi is not my God"—and even forbids the minister from uttering the Emperor's name, treating the imperial threat as empty fear. Yet he cannot fully escape it: the minister reveals that a complaint has already been lodged against him with the Emperor, and Pratapaditya boastfully claims he himself will "arrange the Emperor's punishment."

In Chapter 22, that same imperial specter is turned into a weapon against his son. Bhagavat and Sitaram fabricate a petition falsely portraying the Yubaraj (Udayaditya) as having complained of treason against Pratapaditya to the Emperor in order to seize the kingdom. Because Rukmini's ring bore the Yubaraj's seal, the forgery was convincingly stamped. Bhagavat, instead of taking it to Delhi, delivers it straight to Pratapaditya, claiming he intercepted Udayaditya's servant fleeing toward Delhi with it.

The mechanism is thus one of reversal: the very fear Pratapaditya scorned—imperial displeasure and accusations reaching Delhi—is exploited through forged evidence of his son's treachery. Confronted with seemingly undeniable proof that Udayaditya had appealed to Delhi against him, Pratapaditya turns on his son and imprisons him, while the schemer Bhagavat is rewarded with his old post at the palace.

In Chapter 8, hair-styling is established as Surma's intimate prerogative: dissatisfied with the Mahishi's heavy, ostentatious styling, Vibha secretly goes to Surma to have her hair done to her own liking—a small act of shared taste and complicity between the two young women. The Mahishi immediately reads the hairstyle as Surma's handiwork, accusing her of jealousy and deliberately "ruining" Vibha's hair before undoing and redoing it herself. Thus the arrangement of Vibha's hair becomes a contested text: Surma's touch speaks of affection and youth, while the Mahishi's restyling asserts authority over Vibha's appearance.

After Surma's death in Chapter 18, this same act turns into an emblem of absence: Vibha sits quietly at the time of braiding her hair "as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it for her," waiting until evening falls and the hair remains unbraided. The undone hair is the physical trace of the one who used to perform this daily intimacy, and no one can replace her. The marker persists into Chapter 23, where Rammohan finds Vibha's "hair unkempt," showing that with Surma gone, that daily care—and the joy it embodied—has never been restored. The groomed versus unbraided/unkempt hair thus charts the arc from Surma's living presence to a grief that even time does not repair.
